title: Machine Learning Models
summary: A machine learning model is a mathematical function with learned statistical weights that maps input features to target predictions or generated text.

body.definition: A parameterized mathematical representation generated by an algorithm through training on historical data, capable of making inferences or generating outputs from novel inputs.

body.text: Unlike traditional software where human programmers write explicit conditional `if/else` rules, a machine learning model learns the underlying logic automatically. It consists of an architectural skeleton (such as a neural network topology) combined with millions or billions of numerical floating-point weights.
Model Formats in Production

items: ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange): Cross-platform interoperable format for deploying models across diverse hardware backends.
GGUF / GGML: Highly quantized binary format optimized for CPU and local on-device LLM inference.
SafeTensors: Fast, zero-copy, secure tensor storage format preventing arbitrary Python code execution during model loading.

body.text: Quantization (e.g. INT8 or INT4) shrinks model weights from 16-bit floats to 4-bit integers, drastically reducing RAM requirements with minimal accuracy loss.

title: Model Training & Backpropagation
summary: Training is the iterative optimization process where a model calculates loss errors and adjusts internal weights using gradient descent and backpropagation.

body.definition: An algorithm that computes the mathematical gradient of a loss function with respect to each weight in a neural network using the calculus chain rule.

body.text: During training, input data is fed forward through the network layers to produce a prediction. A Loss Function compares the prediction against ground-truth labels. An optimizer (like AdamW or SGD) uses the calculated gradients to update every weight slightly in the direction that minimizes overall error.
Core Training Concepts

items: Epoch: One complete forward and backward pass through the entire training dataset.
Learning Rate: Hyperparameter controlling the step size taken along the loss gradient during each weight update.
Batch Size: The number of training samples processed concurrently on GPU clusters before calculating a gradient step.

body.text: Training large foundation models requires thousands of specialized GPUs running for weeks across high-speed InfiniBand network clusters.

title: Model Parameters & Weights
summary: Parameters are the internal numerical weights and biases that a neural network adjusts during training to store learned knowledge and associations.

body.definition: An internal numerical coefficient inside a neural network layer that multiplies an incoming signal, adjusted iteratively by optimization algorithms during training.

body.text: When a model is described as '7B' (7 Billion parameters) or '70B', it refers to the total count of individual floating-point numbers that define its neural connections. Storing a 7B parameter model in standard 16-bit precision (FP16 / BF16) requires roughly 14 GB of VRAM just to load the weights.
Parameters vs Hyperparameters

rows.label: Learned By
values: Learned automatically by model from training data
Configured manually by human engineers before training

rows.label: Examples
values: Learning rate, batch size, dropout rate, temperature

rows.label: Modification
values: Updated on every backprop gradient step

body.text: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a fraction of total parameters (e.g. 8 experts routing 2 active per token) during inference to save compute.

title: Tokens & Subword Tokenization
summary: Tokens are the fundamental numerical chunks (characters, subwords, or words) that language models read and generate instead of raw characters.

body.definition: The algorithmic process of segmenting raw text strings into discrete numerical token IDs using a fixed vocabulary dictionary (typically 32k to 128k tokens).

body.text: LLMs do not process text character-by-character or word-by-word. Algorithms like Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) break common words into single tokens (e.g. 'technology' = 1 token) while splitting rare words into subword fragments ('unprecedented' -> 'un', 'preced', 'ented'). In English, 1 token is roughly equivalent to 0.75 words or 4 characters.
Token Processing Pipeline

items: Tokenization: Converts input string into an array of integer token IDs (`[15496, 2038, ...]`).
Embedding Lookup: Maps each token ID into a high-dimensional dense vector space (e.g. 4096 dimensions).
Logits & Sampling: The model outputs a probability distribution across the entire vocabulary to sample the next token.

body.text: Context Window limits (e.g. 128k or 1M tokens) define the maximum combined prompt and generation token capacity a model can attend to simultaneously.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs) & Transformers
summary: LLMs are deep neural networks based on the Transformer architecture trained on trillions of words to predict the most probable next token.

body.definition: A deep neural network architecture introduced in 2017 relying entirely on Self-Attention mechanisms to process input sequences in parallel.

body.text: Before Transformers, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) processed text sequentially, forgetting long-range context. The Self-Attention mechanism allows every token in a prompt to attend directly to every other token simultaneously, capturing complex syntactic, semantic, and logical relationships across thousands of words.
Key Transformer Components

items: Multi-Head Self-Attention: Multiple parallel attention heads computing dynamic relationship matrices across tokens.
Feed-Forward Layers (FFN): Dense neural layers that process and transform token representations.
Positional Encoding (RoPE): Injects sequence order awareness into parallelized attention calculations.

body.text: Temperature sampling controls generation creativity: lower values (0.2) yield deterministic, focused responses, while higher values (0.8) increase variety.

title: Model Inference & KV Cache
summary: Inference is the forward-pass execution of a trained model to generate predictions or stream auto-regressive tokens for end users in real time.

body.definition: The operational production phase where a trained machine learning model accepts live real-world inputs and executes forward mathematical computations to produce outputs.

body.text: Unlike training (which computes gradients and updates weights using backpropagation), inference strictly runs forward passes with static, frozen weights. In LLMs, inference is autoregressive: the model generates one token at a time, appending it to the context and feeding it back into the model for the next token.
Inference Acceleration: The KV Cache

items: Key-Value (KV) Cache: Stores previously computed attention matrices in GPU VRAM so earlier prompt tokens do not need to be recalculated on every new token.
Time to First Token (TTFT): The latency required to process the initial prompt (pre-fill phase).
Tokens Per Second (TPS): The generation speed during the autoregressive decode phase.

body.text: Speculative Decoding uses a small, fast draft model to predict candidate tokens, which the larger primary model verifies in parallel in a single forward step.

title: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs)
summary: Neural networks are computational models loosely inspired by biological brains, connecting layers of artificial neurons with non-linear activation functions.

body.definition: A computational architecture composed of interconnected nodes ('neurons') grouped into layers, where each connection transmits a weighted signal activated by a non-linear function.

body.text: A standard neural network consists of an Input Layer, multiple Hidden Layers (Deep Learning), and an Output Layer. Each neuron sums its weighted inputs (`sum(w_i * x_i) + bias`) and passes the sum through an activation function like ReLU, GELU, or Sigmoid to introduce non-linearity.
Common Activation Functions
Non-linear activation functions allow neural networks to approximate any continuous mathematical function (Universal Approximation Theorem).

title: Overfitting vs Underfitting
summary: Overfitting happens when a model memorizes training noise and outliers, failing to generalize to new, unseen validation data.

body.definition: A machine learning modeling error occurring when a function corresponds too closely to a specific training dataset, capturing random noise rather than true underlying statistical patterns.

body.text: An overfitted model achieves 99% accuracy on training data but performs poorly in real-world deployment. In contrast, an underfitted model is too simplistic to capture the core relationships. Machine learning engineering focuses on finding the optimal sweet spot that minimizes validation loss.
Techniques to Prevent Overfitting

items: Dropout: Randomly deactivating a fraction (e.g. 10-20%) of neurons during each training step to prevent co-adaptation.
Weight Decay (L2 Regularization): Penalizing large weight values in the loss function to encourage simpler decision boundaries.
Early Stopping: Halting training when validation loss stops improving, even if training loss continues downward.
Data Augmentation: Artificially expanding datasets by rotating, cropping, or adding noise to samples.

body.text: Cross-validation (k-fold) splits data into k subsets, ensuring every sample serves as both training and validation data across iterations.

title: Datasets: Train, Validation & Test Splits
summary: A dataset is a curated collection of data samples partitioned into Training, Validation, and Test sets to build and objectively evaluate models.

body.definition: The standard practice of dividing an initial dataset into distinct subsets (typically 80/10/10) to train parameters, tune hyperparameters, and test final generalization.

body.text: Data quality is the single largest determinant of model capability ('garbage in, garbage out'). Pre-processing pipelines clean datasets by deduplicating identical samples, filtering toxic content, normalizing text formatting, and balancing class representation.
Standard Dataset Splits

items: Training Set (70-80%): Directly ingested by backpropagation algorithms to update internal weights.
Validation Set (10-15%): Evaluated after each epoch to tune hyperparameters and trigger early stopping without contaminating test evaluation.
Test Set (10-15%): Kept strictly locked away until final development is complete to provide an unbiased benchmark of true real-world accuracy.

body.text: Data contamination occurs when test questions accidentally leak into the pre-training corpus, producing artificially inflated benchmark scores.

title: Prompt Engineering & Few-Shot In-Context Learning
summary: Prompt engineering structures natural language instructions and context to steer LLM outputs without modifying internal model weights.

body.definition: The emergent ability of foundation LLMs to learn tasks and format patterns dynamically from instructions and examples provided within the prompt context window.

body.text: Because LLMs are probabilistic token predictors, the phrasing, structure, and formatting of an input prompt significantly affect the quality of the generated completion. Prompt engineering combines role-prompting, few-shot demonstration exemplars, and structured chain-of-thought constraints.
Core Prompting Paradigms

items: Zero-Shot: Directly instructing the model to perform a task with no prior examples.
Few-Shot: Providing 2-5 example input/output pairs inside the prompt to anchor desired formatting and tone.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT): Encouraging the model to output step-by-step reasoning ('think step by step') before outputting final answers to improve mathematical accuracy.

body.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fetches relevant chunks from external vector databases, injecting real-time factual context into the prompt.

title: Fine-Tuning & Parameter-Efficient LoRA
summary: Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained base model on domain-specific datasets, adapting its weights for specialized tasks and style formatting.

body.definition: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) technique that freezes base model weights and trains small low-rank decomposition rank-matrices inside attention layers.

body.text: Pre-training creates generalist 'base models' by ingesting trillions of internet tokens. Fine-tuning uses Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF / DPO) to transform the base predictor into a helpful, instruction-following assistant.

title: Supervised vs Unsupervised vs Reinforcement Learning
summary: Supervised learning learns from labeled input-output pairs, unsupervised learning discovers hidden data clusters, and reinforcement learning optimizes rewards.

body.definition: A machine learning paradigm where an autonomous agent learns to make sequences of decisions by interacting with an environment to maximize cumulative reward feedback.

body.text: All machine learning paradigms fall into three core pillars based on feedback signals: direct teacher supervision with ground-truth labels, autonomous discovery of latent structure without labels, or trial-and-error environmental reward maximization.
The Three Learning Pillars

rows.label: Supervised Learning
values: Spam detection, medical imaging diagnostics, translation

rows.label: Unsupervised Learning
values: Customer segmentation, anomaly detection, dimension reduction

rows.label: Reinforcement Learning
values: Robotics control, game AI (AlphaGo, chess), self-driving cars

body.text: Self-Supervised Learning (used in LLMs) automatically creates its own supervisory labels from raw text by hiding words and learning to fill in the blanks.
